intro: Long before there was a place called Illinois, there was a city. Around the year 1100, tens of thousands of people lived, farmed and traded at Cahokia, on the Mississippi River. They raised a mound of earth taller than a ten-story building. They built it one basket of dirt at a time. Cahokia was only one of hundreds of nations that lived across North America, each one shaped by its own land: forests, plains, deserts, coasts and ice.

Then, in 1492, ships crossed the Atlantic. What followed changed both sides of the ocean. Corn and potatoes fed Europe. Horses changed the Plains. Diseases killed more people than any war. Spanish soldiers, French traders and English farmers each treated the peoples they met differently. Native nations fought, made deals, adapted and survived.

In this unit you will learn how the land shaped Native ways of life, what the meeting of two worlds cost and carried, and how to read a source by asking who wrote it and why. You will end able to explain the same event from more than one point of view, using real evidence.
bigQuestion: How did the land shape the first peoples of North America, and how did meeting Europeans change both worlds?

test.q: How do scientists know people lived in North America at least fifteen thousand years ago?
choices: From stone tools found with the bones of ice age animals
test.why: Spear points found with mammoth bones can be dated, and they show people were here long before any writing.

choices: Pueblos of mud brick in the Southwest
test.why: Southwest peoples built with stone and mud brick because there was little wood and the thick walls stayed cool.

test.q: Why did Plains peoples move during the year?
test.why: Their food, clothing and shelter came from bison, and the herds moved with the seasons.

test.q: What fed the city of Cahokia?
choices: Corn grown in the river bottom
test.why: Rich soil and corn farming let thousands of people live in one place.

test.q: What role did clan mothers play among the Haudenosaunee?
choices: They chose and could remove chiefs
test.why: The senior women of each clan picked the chiefs who sat on the Grand Council.

test.q: Copper from Lake Superior and shells from the Gulf of Mexico at Cahokia show that
choices: trade routes stretched hundreds of miles
test.why: Neither item is found near Cahokia, so both had to arrive by long-distance trade.

test.q: Which is true of Native nations today?
choices: They are sovereign nations with their own governments
test.why: More than five hundred seventy nations are recognized, and many Native people live in cities like Chicago.

test.q: Why did Columbus sail west in 1492?
choices: To reach Asia and its spices by a new route
test.why: He believed Asia was a short sail west and that he could reach its trade goods directly.

test.q: Which pair shows the Columbian Exchange going in opposite directions?
choices: Corn to Europe and horses to the Americas
Wheat to Europe and cattle to the Americas
Potatoes to Europe and tomatoes to the Americas
Horses to Europe and pigs to the Americas
test.why: Corn was an American crop that went east, and horses were a European animal that came west.

test.q: Why did smallpox kill so many more Native people than Europeans?
choices: Native people lived in bigger cities
Native people had never met the germ and had no immunity
The disease was different in the Americas
test.why: Immunity comes from earlier exposure, and no one in the Americas had ever been exposed.

test.q: Which matches the country with how it usually treated Native peoples?
choices: Spain: traded furs and married in
England: built missions and forced labor
France: traded furs and made alliances
test.why: The few French who came depended on Native hunters, so they built alliances and trading posts.

test.q: Who led the 1680 uprising that drove the Spanish out of New Mexico?
test.why: Popé sent knotted cords to the pueblos so they would rise on the same day.

test.q: What did the Treaty of Chicago in 1833 do?
choices: Took the Potawatomi's last land in northern Illinois
test.why: After the treaty the Potawatomi were removed west, and almost no Native land was left in Illinois.

test.q: Learning to ride horses and to read treaties are examples of
test.why: Native nations took new tools and skills to protect themselves, which is adapting, not surrender.

test.q: Why should you ask who wrote a source and why?
choices: To find out if it is old
Because the writer's point of view shapes what the source says
Because only old sources are true
test.why: Columbus wrote to impress a king; Black Hawk spoke to explain a defeat. Purpose shapes every source.

write.prompt: Pick one Native nation or region from this unit. Make a claim about the biggest way meeting Europeans changed that nation's life. Support it with evidence from the readings, sources and data in the unit.
tips: Claim: state your answer in one sentence. Example: 'The horse changed Plains life more than anything else.'
Evidence: use at least two facts from the unit, such as a date, a number from a data table or a line from a source.
Reasoning: explain how each piece of evidence supports your claim, not just that it does.
The other side: name one different change someone could argue was bigger, and say why yours is stronger.
Point of view: say whose story your evidence comes from, and what the other side might add.

title: The First Peoples of North America

chapters.title: Nations Across the Continent
chapters.bigQuestion: How did the land shape the many different ways Native peoples lived across North America?

story.title: Market Day Under the Great Mound
story.kicker: Around the year 1100, the biggest city north of Mexico stood beside the Mississippi River, a short walk from where St. Louis is today.
paragraphs: The sun comes up over the river, and the city is already awake. A girl named Little Fawn walks with her mother toward the great plaza. Smoke rises from hundreds of houses with thatched roofs. Ahead of them stands a mound of earth taller than any tree. On top of it sits the house of the city's leader. Little Fawn has climbed the steps of that mound only once, on a feast day.

The plaza is bigger than a whole village. It is packed with people. Some have walked in from farms a day away. Others came by canoe from far up the river. Little Fawn hears words she does not know. Traders from the south have brought seashells. Traders from the north have brought copper that shines like the sun. Her mother trades a basket of dried corn for a small copper bead.

In one corner of the plaza, men are playing chunkey. One player rolls a smooth stone disk across the ground. Two others throw long poles, trying to land closest to where the disk will stop. A crowd shouts and bets on the game. Little Fawn knows this game is played in villages hundreds of miles away. Cahokia's ideas travel as far as its traders do.

Near the edge of the city, Little Fawn passes a circle of tall wooden posts. A priest watches the sun through the posts to track the seasons. He will tell the farmers when to plant. Corn, beans and squash feed this city of thousands. Without them, there would be no plaza, no mound and no market.

Nobody in Little Fawn's world writes anything down. So how do we know about her city? Archaeologists dig into the soil and find house posts, broken pots, corn cobs, shell beads and copper. They measure the mounds. They count the houses. From those clues, they rebuild a day like this one. Cahokia's people left no books, but they left a city.
story.think: Cahokia had no writing. What kinds of things would you look for in the ground if you wanted to learn how its people lived?

lessons.title: The First People Arrive
lessons.mainIdea: People have lived in North America for at least fifteen thousand years, and we know it from the tools and bones they left behind.
reading: Long before any city, people walked and paddled into North America. Most scientists think they came from Asia. During the last *ice age*, so much water was frozen in ice that the sea was lower. Land connected Asia and Alaska. People may have crossed that land, or paddled along the coast. This happened at least fifteen thousand years ago. Some sites may be older.

How do we know? Nobody wrote it down. Instead, people left things behind. Near Clovis, New Mexico, hunters made long stone spear points. They dropped them next to the bones of mammoths. Scientists call these *artifacts*, objects that people made. They can tell how old an artifact is by testing the bone or charcoal found with it.

Illinois has these clues too. Farmers plowing fields have turned up stone spear points thousands of years old. Along the rivers, people fished and gathered nuts. Slowly they learned to grow plants. By about a thousand years ago, corn had become the main food in many places. That change made villages and cities possible.

words.d: a long time when much of Earth was covered by ice and the sea was lower
an object made or used by people long ago, such as a spear point or pot

look.title: A Spear Point in a Cornfield
look.text: A farmer in central Illinois picks up a gray stone from a plowed field. It is shaped like a leaf, with sharp edges and a groove at the base. A scientist says it is about ten thousand years old. No one has lived on that spot, as far as anyone knows, for a very long time.
look.prompt: What can this one stone tell us about the people who made it? What can it not tell us?

check.q: How long have people lived in North America?
check.why: The oldest sites are at least fifteen thousand years old, and some may be older.

check.q: Why could people walk from Asia to Alaska during the ice age?
choices: The sea was lower, so land was uncovered
The two places were always joined
check.why: So much water was frozen that the sea dropped, and land connected the two continents.

check.q: What is an artifact?
choices: An object made or used by people long ago
check.why: Artifacts are objects people made, like spear points and pots, and they are our main clues about people without writing.

lessons.title: Many Lands, Many Ways
lessons.mainIdea: Native peoples lived in hundreds of nations, each with its own language and its own way of living that fit its land.
reading: When Europeans arrived in the 1490s, millions of people already lived in North America. They did not belong to one group. They belonged to hundreds of *nations*. A nation is a people with its own land, its own leaders and its own language. The Lakota, the Hopi and the Haudenosaunee were as different from each other as Spain is from China.

The land shaped how each nation lived. In the forests of the east, people built homes from bark and grew corn. On the grassy plains, people hunted bison. In the dry Southwest, people built with mud brick and watered their crops by hand. On the rainy northwest coast, people fished for salmon and carved giant cedar trees. In the frozen north, people hunted seals on the ice.

Scientists call each of these areas a *culture region*. Nations in the same region often shared foods, homes and tools, because they faced the same weather and the same plants and animals. But they still had their own languages and stories. In this chapter you will visit five regions and one great city. Keep asking one question: how did the land shape the way people lived?

words.d: a people with its own land, leaders and language
a large area where peoples shared similar foods, homes and tools because of the land

look.title: Rain Across the Regions
look.unit: inches of rain or melted snow per year, rough
look.cite: Rounded typical figures for each region; National Weather Service averages
look.prompt: Which region would be easiest for growing corn? Which would be hardest? How might that change what people ate?

check.q: What is a nation?
choices: A people with its own land, leaders and language
check.why: Each Native nation had its own land, leaders and language, and there were hundreds of them.

check.q: Why did nations in the same region often share foods and homes?
choices: They faced the same weather, plants and animals
check.why: The same land gives the same materials and foods, so peoples in one region solved problems in similar ways.

check.q: Based on the rain data, where would farming be hardest?
check.why: The Arctic gets only about six inches of moisture a year and is frozen most of the year, so crops cannot grow there.

lessons.title: Longhouses of the Eastern Woodlands
lessons.mainIdea: In the eastern forests, people built longhouses from bark and grew corn, beans and squash together.
reading: Picture a forest of oak and maple that goes on for weeks of walking. This was the Eastern Woodlands, from the Atlantic coast to the Mississippi River. Wood was everywhere, so people built with it. The Haudenosaunee of what is now New York built *longhouses*. A longhouse had a frame of bent poles covered with sheets of elm bark. It could be as long as a school hallway.

Several related families lived in one longhouse. Each family had its own space along the wall, with a shared fire in the middle. The oldest woman in the family was in charge of the house. Other Woodlands peoples, like the Algonquian nations, built smaller round homes called wigwams. Both kinds of home used bark, because bark was free and easy to find.

Woodlands farmers planted three crops in the same mound of soil. They called them the *three sisters*: corn, beans and squash. The corn grew tall. The beans climbed the corn stalks. The squash spread its wide leaves on the ground and kept the soil damp. Beans also put back into the soil what corn used up. Together, the three sisters fed whole villages. Corn from these fields still shapes what Illinois grows today.

words.d: a long home with a pole frame and bark walls, shared by several related families
corn, beans and squash, planted together in one mound so each helps the others

look.title: Three Plants in One Mound
look.text: A Woodlands farmer pushes corn seeds into a small hill of soil. A few weeks later she plants beans beside the young corn. Then she plants squash around the edge. By late summer the corn is taller than she is, beans hang from the stalks, and huge squash leaves shade the ground so weeds cannot grow.
look.prompt: Why is planting the three crops together smarter than planting each in its own field?

check.q: What were longhouses made of?
choices: Bent poles and sheets of bark
check.why: The Woodlands were full of trees, so people built homes from poles and elm bark.

check.q: What did the beans do for the corn?
choices: They climbed the stalks and put good things back in the soil
check.why: Beans used the corn as a pole to climb, and they returned to the soil what the corn had used up.

check.q: Who was in charge of a Haudenosaunee longhouse?
choices: The chief of the whole nation
The oldest woman in the family
check.why: Longhouses belonged to the women of a family, and the oldest woman led the household.

lessons.title: Bison and Tipis on the Plains
lessons.mainIdea: On the treeless Great Plains, people depended on the bison for food, shelter, clothing and tools.
reading: West of the Mississippi the trees thin out. Then they stop. The Great Plains are a sea of grass that stretches from Texas to Canada. Millions of *bison*, the big shaggy animals many people call buffalo, grazed on that grass. Before Europeans came, there were tens of millions of them. For the peoples of the Plains, the bison was life.

Plains peoples used every part of the animal. Meat was eaten fresh or dried for winter. Hides became blankets, robes and the walls of homes. Bones became tools and needles. Horns became spoons. Even the stomach could be a cooking pot. Wasting a bison was unthinkable, because the whole village depended on it.

Bison herds moved with the seasons, so many Plains peoples moved too. Their home was the *tipi*, a cone of long poles covered with bison hides. A tipi could be taken down in minutes and packed onto a dog sled. Before Europeans brought horses, dogs did the hauling. Nations like the Lakota and Cheyenne followed the herds across the grass, and their homes came with them.

words.d: a large, shaggy grazing animal of the Plains, often called a buffalo
a cone-shaped home of poles and bison hides that could be moved quickly

look.title: Where the Bison Went
look.cite: Standard estimates used by the National Park Service and historians, rounded
look.prompt: What happened to the bison between 1870 and 1890? What would that have meant for people who depended on them?

check.q: Why did many Plains peoples move their homes during the year?
check.why: Bison moved with the seasons, and the people who depended on them moved too.

check.q: Before horses arrived, what carried a packed-up tipi?
check.why: Dogs pulled loads on small sleds until Europeans brought horses.

check.q: Which of these was NOT made from bison?
check.why: Bark canoes came from Woodlands trees. Hides made tipi walls, bones made needles, and horns made spoons.

lessons.title: Pueblos and Ditches of the Southwest
lessons.mainIdea: In the dry Southwest, people built towns of stone and mud brick and dug ditches to bring water to their corn.
reading: Now picture red cliffs, dry ground and a hot sun. This is the Southwest, in what is now Arizona and New Mexico. Rain is rare. Yet people have farmed here for more than two thousand years. The Ancestral Puebloans, the Hopi, the Zuni and others built towns of stone and mud brick. The Spanish later called these towns *pueblos*, their word for villages.

A pueblo looked like an apartment building made of earth. Rooms were stacked several stories high. People climbed ladders to reach the upper floors. Thick walls kept rooms cool in the day and warm at night. Some pueblos were built into the sides of cliffs, high above the valley floor. Others, like Acoma in New Mexico, sit on top of a mesa and have been lived in for hundreds of years.

Farming with so little rain took skill. People dug ditches to carry river water to their fields. This is called *irrigation*. They planted corn deep in the ground where the soil stayed damp. They saved seeds from the plants that survived dry years. Corn, beans and squash grew here too, along with cotton for clothes. The Hopi still plant corn in the desert today, using ways their families have kept for centuries.

words.d: a town of stone and mud brick with rooms stacked several stories high
bringing water to fields through ditches or canals

look.title: A Town in the Cliff
look.text: High on a cliff in southwest Colorado, stone rooms are tucked under a rock overhang. The rooms were built about eight hundred years ago. To get in, families climbed hand and toe holds cut into the cliff. From the doorways you can see the whole valley below.
look.prompt: Why might people choose to build their homes high in a cliff instead of down by the fields?

check.q: What is irrigation?
choices: Climbing a ladder to a roof
Saving seeds for the next year
Bringing water to fields through ditches
check.why: Southwest farmers dug ditches to carry river water to their crops because rain was rare.

check.q: Why did thick pueblo walls help people?
choices: They kept rooms cool by day and warm at night
check.why: Thick earth walls hold steady heat, which matters in a desert with hot days and cold nights.

check.q: Which peoples still live in pueblos in the Southwest today?
check.why: The Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblo peoples have lived in the Southwest for many centuries and still do.

lessons.title: Cedar and Salmon on the Northwest Coast
lessons.mainIdea: On the rainy Pacific Northwest coast, giant cedar trees and rivers full of salmon made rich villages possible.
reading: On the Pacific coast, from Oregon up to Alaska, it rains most of the year. Giant cedar trees grow taller than a ten-story building. Every spring and fall, rivers fill with *salmon* swimming upstream to lay their eggs. Peoples like the Haida, Tlingit and Chinook had so much food that they did not need to farm. They caught salmon by the thousands and dried and smoked them for winter.

Cedar was the wood for everything. People split the soft, straight-grained trunks into planks and built large houses. They hollowed whole logs into canoes that could go out on the ocean. They wove cedar bark into clothes, mats and baskets. And they carved tall cedar posts with animals and family symbols. These are the *totem poles* that stood in front of homes.

A totem pole is not a god or an idol. It is a family record. The carved raven, bear or whale shows the family's history and its rights. Rich families held a feast called a potlatch. The host gave away blankets, food and other gifts to hundreds of guests. Giving more away showed more honor. In this land of plenty, being generous was the way to become great.

words.d: a fish that swims from the ocean up rivers each year, the main food of the Northwest coast
a tall carved cedar post showing a family's animals, history and rights

look.title: The Day the River Turned Silver
look.text: In late summer a Chinook boy stands on a wooden platform over a rushing river. Below him the water is so thick with salmon that it flashes silver. His uncle dips a net and lifts out three fish at once. By nightfall the drying racks are full. There will be food all winter without planting a single seed.
look.prompt: Why did people here have time to carve, build and hold big feasts when Plains peoples had to keep moving?

check.q: Why did Northwest coast peoples not need to farm?
choices: Rivers full of salmon gave them plenty of food
They traded with the Plains for food
It was too cold for plants
check.why: The salmon runs gave so much food that people could dry and store enough for the whole year.

check.q: What does a totem pole show?
choices: A family's animals, history and rights
check.why: The carved animals are family symbols that tell the family's story and what it is entitled to.

check.q: At a potlatch, how did a host show honor?
check.why: Giving wealth away to guests was the way a family earned respect on the Northwest coast.

lessons.title: Ice and Sea in the Arctic
lessons.mainIdea: In the Arctic, where nothing can be farmed, the Inuit lived by hunting seals and whales and inventing tools for ice and sea.
reading: At the top of the continent, the ground stays frozen all year. No trees grow. In winter the sun barely rises. This is the Arctic, home of the Inuit and their relatives across Alaska, Canada and Greenland. You cannot farm here. But the sea is full of life. Seals, walrus, whales and fish became food, fuel and clothing.

Inuit inventions fit this world exactly. The *kayak* was a light one-person boat with a skin cover stretched over a frame. A hunter sat inside, sealed against the icy water. Sleds pulled by dogs crossed the snow. Boots and parkas were sewn from seal and caribou skins with sinew thread. Seal oil burned in stone lamps for light and heat.

In winter some Inuit families built domed houses from blocks of packed snow. The snow held in body heat. In summer they lived in tents of skin. They knew the ice the way a farmer knows a field: which ice would hold, which would break, where seals came up to breathe. Today Inuit still hunt in the Arctic, often by snowmobile, and their languages are still spoken.

words.d: the far north around the North Pole, where the ground stays frozen and no trees grow
a light, covered one-person boat with a skin cover over a frame

look.title: Waiting at the Breathing Hole
look.text: An Inuit hunter stands still on the sea ice with a spear. In front of him is a small hole in the ice. Under the ice, a seal must come up to breathe every few minutes. It might use this hole. The hunter has waited two hours. His parka is seal skin. His boots are caribou. His spear tip is walrus tusk.
look.prompt: Count the animals this hunter depends on just to stand there. What would happen to his family if the seals disappeared?

check.q: Why could Inuit not farm?
choices: The ground stays frozen all year
check.why: Frozen ground and a dark, cold winter make farming impossible in the Arctic.

check.q: What is a kayak?
choices: A light covered boat for one person
check.why: The kayak was a skin-covered boat that let a hunter go out on icy water without getting wet.

check.q: Why did a snow house stay warm inside?
choices: A big wood fire burned inside
The sun shone through the walls
Packed snow held in the people's body heat
The walls were made of seal skin
check.why: Snow traps air, so a snow dome holds in warmth from bodies and a small oil lamp. There was no wood to burn.

lessons.title: Cahokia, a City of Mounds
lessons.mainIdea: Around the year 1100, Cahokia in Illinois was the largest city north of Mexico, built by farmers who raised huge mounds of earth.
reading: Cahokia stood on the east side of the Mississippi River, across from what is now St. Louis. It was in Illinois. Around the year 1100 it may have held ten thousand to twenty thousand people. No city in the United States would be that big again until Philadelphia in the 1700s. Its people belonged to a way of life scientists call Mississippian.

The city was famous for its *mounds*. People carried soil in baskets, one load at a time, and piled it up. The biggest, now called Monks Mound, is about one hundred feet tall. Its base covers about fourteen acres, more than ten football fields. About one hundred twenty mounds once stood in the city. Leaders lived on top of some. Others held the dead.

Corn made Cahokia possible. Farmers in the rich river bottom grew enough to feed thousands of people who did not farm: builders, priests, potters, traders. By about 1350, the city was empty. Nobody knows exactly why. Floods, crop failures, war and worn-out soil are all possible. The mounds still stand at Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site, and you can climb Monks Mound today.

words.d: a hill made by people piling up earth, basket by basket
the way of life of the corn-farming, mound-building peoples of the Mississippi valley around 800 to 1500

look.title: Cahokia by the Numbers
rows: Base of Monks Mound in acres
People at its peak, low estimate
People at its peak, high estimate
look.unit: feet, acres, mounds or people, rounded
look.cite: Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site; standard estimates, rounded
look.prompt: Every basket of dirt in Monks Mound was carried by a person. What does that tell you about how Cahokia's people were organized?

check.q: Where was Cahokia?
choices: In Illinois, across the river from St. Louis
check.why: Cahokia stood in the Mississippi river bottom in southern Illinois.

check.q: How were the mounds built?
choices: People carried soil in baskets and piled it up
check.why: There were no horses or wheels. People carried the earth one basket at a time.

check.q: What made it possible for a city of thousands to exist?
choices: Corn farming in the rich river soil
check.why: Corn from the river bottom fed the many people who built, traded and led instead of farming.

lessons.title: The Haudenosaunee Council
lessons.mainIdea: Five nations in the Northeast joined under the Great Law of Peace, with a council that decided together and clan mothers who chose the leaders.
reading: Long before the United States, five nations in what is now New York State were at war with each other. According to their own history, a man called the Peacemaker traveled among them. He urged them to stop fighting and join together. The Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca agreed. They called themselves the Haudenosaunee, the people of the longhouse. Later the Tuscarora joined as a sixth nation.

Their agreement is called the Great Law of Peace. It set up a *confederacy*, a group of nations that stay separate but act together on big matters. Each nation sent chiefs to a Grand Council. The council met at Onondaga, in the middle. Chiefs talked until they agreed. No one nation could force the others. A war against one was a war against all.

Women held real power. Each family belonged to a clan, and the oldest women, the *clan mothers*, chose the chiefs. If a chief did wrong, a clan mother could remove him. Some early Americans, including Benjamin Franklin, knew about the council and admired how the nations worked together. The Haudenosaunee Grand Council still meets today.

words.d: a group of nations that stay separate but join together to act on big decisions
the senior woman of a clan, who chose and could remove chiefs

look.title: Words of the Great Law
look.text: The Great Law of Peace, passed down by speech and wampum, says that the chiefs of the council must have skin seven spans thick, so that anger and hard words do not pierce them. It tells leaders to think not of themselves, but of the people to come, even the children not yet born.
look.cite: Haudenosaunee Great Law of Peace, oral tradition first written down in the 1800s (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What does it mean for a leader to have skin seven spans thick? Why would a council want leaders like that?

check.q: What did the Great Law of Peace do?
choices: Made one nation rule the others
Joined five nations in a confederacy that decided together
check.why: The five nations stayed separate but agreed to act together and stop fighting each other.

check.q: Who chose the chiefs?
check.why: The senior women of each clan chose the chiefs and could remove them.

check.q: Which nation joined the confederacy later as the sixth?
check.why: The original five were Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca. The Tuscarora joined in the 1700s.

lessons.title: Stories, Art and Trade Routes
lessons.mainIdea: Native peoples passed down knowledge through spoken stories and art, and traded goods across thousands of miles.
reading: Most Native nations did not use writing. Instead, they kept their history by *oral tradition*, passing stories from one generation to the next by speech. Elders told how the world began, how the clan got its name and where the boundaries were. Children heard the stories many times until they knew them. A good storyteller was as important as a good hunter.

Art carried memory too. The Haudenosaunee wove beads of white and purple shell into belts called *wampum*. A wampum belt recorded a treaty or an important event. Its pattern was read aloud at council. Plains peoples painted the year's big event on a bison hide, adding one picture each winter. Pueblo potters painted designs that told who made the pot and where.

Trade tied the continent together. Archaeologists at Cahokia have found copper from Lake Superior, seashells from the Gulf of Mexico and a shiny stone from the Rocky Mountains. Each of these traveled hundreds of miles by canoe and on foot. Goods, ideas and games moved along the same paths. When Europeans arrived, they walked onto trails that were already old.

words.d: history and knowledge kept by telling it aloud from one generation to the next
belts of white and purple shell beads used to record treaties and events

look.title: An Early Visitor Sees the Mounds
look.text: In 1811 an American traveler named Henry Brackenridge walked among the mounds at Cahokia. He wrote that when he came to the great mound, he was struck with astonishment. He said that a city of thousands must have stood there, and that raising such a work must have taken years of labor by many people.
look.cite: Henry Brackenridge, letter and travel writing, 1811 to 1814 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Brackenridge saw the mounds but not the people. What clues did he use to guess that a large city had stood there?

check.q: What is oral tradition?
check.why: Without writing, people kept their history by telling it aloud and having the young learn it.

check.q: What does copper from Lake Superior found at Cahokia prove?
choices: Cahokia's people were from the north
Trade goods traveled hundreds of miles
check.why: Lake Superior is far from Cahokia, so the copper had to be carried there by trade.

check.q: What was a wampum belt used for?
choices: Recording a treaty or important event
check.why: The bead patterns recorded agreements and were read aloud at council meetings.

lessons.title: Native Nations Today
lessons.mainIdea: Native nations are still here: more than five hundred are recognized by the United States, and tens of thousands of Native people live in Illinois, many in Chicago.
reading: Native peoples are not only part of the past. Today the United States recognizes more than five hundred seventy Native nations. Each is a *sovereign* nation, which means it has its own government, laws and leaders. Many have their own lands, called reservations. Others do not. Their citizens are also citizens of the United States.

Illinois is named for the Illinois people, who called themselves the Illiniwek. Most of their descendants were pushed west in the 1800s and now belong to the Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma. The Potawatomi, Kickapoo, Miami, Sauk, Meskwaki and Ho-Chunk also lived here. In recent years the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation regained some of its land in northern Illinois.

Chicago today has one of the largest urban Native populations in the country. Native people from many nations moved there for work in the 1900s. The American Indian Center of Chicago, founded in 1953, holds a powwow every year. Native students go to Chicago schools. Native artists, doctors and lawyers work across the state. The first peoples are still here, still speaking, still building.

words.d: having the right to govern itself with its own laws and leaders
land that belongs to a Native nation and is governed by it
a gathering with dancing, drumming and singing where Native people from many nations meet

look.title: A Powwow on the North Side
look.text: On a fall weekend in Chicago, a drum sounds in a park. Dancers in beaded and feathered outfits move in a circle. One dancer is Lakota. Another is Ojibwe. Another is Navajo. A grandmother sells fry bread. A teenager checks her phone between dances. A city bus rolls by on the street.
look.prompt: What in this scene is old, and what is new? Why is it a mistake to think of Native people only as part of the past?

check.q: What does it mean that a Native nation is sovereign?
choices: It is part of the past
It has its own government and laws
check.why: Sovereign means self-governing. Recognized Native nations run their own governments.

check.q: Where do most descendants of the Illinois people live today?
check.why: The Illinois were pushed west in the 1800s, and their descendants are the Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma.

check.q: About how many Native nations does the United States recognize today?
check.why: There are more than five hundred seventy federally recognized nations, each with its own government.

review.q: What is the main way we know about people who lived here before writing?
choices: Artifacts like spear points and pots found in the ground
review.why: Artifacts, mounds and bones are the evidence scientists use to learn about people who did not write.

review.q: Which region's peoples lived mainly by hunting bison?
review.why: Tens of millions of bison lived on the Plains, and Plains peoples used every part of them.

review.q: Why did Southwest peoples use irrigation?
choices: To water crops in a land with little rain
review.why: Rain is rare in the Southwest, so farmers dug ditches to bring river water to their corn.

review.q: Which best explains why homes differed from region to region?
choices: One leader chose each home style
All peoples used the same wood
People built with what their land provided
review.why: Bark in the forests, hides on the Plains, mud brick in the desert, cedar on the coast, snow in the Arctic.

review.q: Which of these was true of Cahokia around the year 1100?
choices: It was the largest city north of Mexico
It was built by the Spanish
It was on the Pacific coast
review.why: Cahokia held ten to twenty thousand people fed by corn farming in the Mississippi valley.

review.q: How did the Haudenosaunee Grand Council make decisions?
choices: Chiefs from each nation talked until they agreed
review.why: No nation could force the others. The chiefs discussed until they reached agreement.

review.q: Seashells from the Gulf of Mexico were found at Cahokia. What does this show?
choices: The shells were dropped by birds
Trade routes reached hundreds of miles
review.why: The Gulf is far south of Illinois, so the shells reached Cahokia by long-distance trade.

review.q: Which statement about Native people today is correct?
choices: They no longer exist as nations
They live only in the West
More than five hundred seventy nations are recognized, and many Native people live in cities like Chicago
review.why: Native nations are sovereign today, and Chicago has one of the largest urban Native populations.

chapters.title: Encounter and Change
chapters.bigQuestion: When Europeans and Native peoples met, what changed for each of them, and who got to tell the story?

story.title: Furs and Kettles on the River
story.kicker: In the winter of 1680, a French trader and an Illinois family met on the Illinois River, and each of them wanted something the other had.
paragraphs: The canoe scrapes onto the frozen mud near where Peoria stands today. A Frenchman named Pierre climbs out, stamping his cold feet. He has paddled from the north with three companions. In his canoe are iron kettles, steel knives, glass beads, wool blankets and a musket. He has come to trade. Up the bank is a village of the Illinois people, hundreds of long houses covered with woven mats.

A man named Chicagou walks down to meet him with his wife, Keewatin, and their son. They have met French traders before. Chicagou carries beaver pelts, soft and thick from the winter. Beaver fur is worth a lot in Paris, where hat makers pay silver for it. Pierre knows this. Chicagou knows Pierre knows it. They begin to talk, half in French, half in the Illinois language, with a lot of hand signs.

Keewatin wants the kettle. Her clay pots crack in the fire and take days to make. An iron kettle lasts for years. Chicagou wants the knife and the musket. A steel blade cuts faster than stone. A musket can kill a deer from far away, and it can frighten an enemy. Pierre wants as many beaver pelts as he can carry. They argue politely for an hour. In the end, both sides walk away pleased.

That evening Pierre eats corn and venison in the family's house. He has learned to smoke the long pipe that the Illinois offer to guests. It means peace. He tells them that a French leader named La Salle is building a fort nearby. Chicagou nods. More French means more kettles. It might also mean more of the sickness that has emptied some villages. He does not say this out loud.

Pierre and Chicagou are made-up names, but this trade really happened, thousands of times, all along the rivers of Illinois. The French wrote about it in their letters and journals. The Illinois told about it in their own stories. Both sides gained, and both sides lost. That is the story of this chapter.
story.think: Pierre and Chicagou both walked away happy. What might each of them lose in the years ahead that they could not see on that day?

lessons.title: Spices, Gold and God
lessons.mainIdea: Europeans in the 1400s wanted a sea route to Asia for trade, and they also wanted gold, land and converts to their religion.
reading: In the 1400s a pinch of pepper in Europe was worth more than its weight in silver. Pepper, cinnamon and cloves came from Asia. So did silk. The goods traveled thousands of miles by land, and every merchant along the way raised the price. European kings and merchants wanted a cheaper way. They wanted to sail to Asia and buy the *spices* directly.

Portugal tried first. Its sailors crept down the coast of Africa, year after year. In 1488 a Portuguese captain rounded the southern tip of Africa. In 1498 another reached India by sea. Spain, Portugal's rival, wanted its own route. A sailor from Italy named Christopher Columbus had an idea. He would sail west, across the ocean, and reach Asia from the other side.

Trade was not the only reason. Europeans also wanted gold, because gold was money. They wanted land, because land made a family rich. And many wanted to spread their religion, *Christianity*. Priests sailed with the soldiers. One historian summed up the reasons as gold, God and glory. All three were on the ships that sailed west.

words.d: plant products like pepper and cinnamon used to flavor food, very costly in Europe
the religion of most Europeans, which many wanted to spread to new lands

look.title: The Price of Pepper
look.text: A sack of pepper leaves India on a ship. It is unloaded and carried by camel across a desert. It is sold to a new merchant in a city on the Mediterranean Sea. Then it is shipped to Italy, and sold again. Then it goes over the mountains to Germany. At every step, someone adds a fee. By the time a cook in Germany buys a pinch, it costs twenty times what it cost in India.
look.prompt: If you could sail straight from Europe to India and skip all those middle steps, what would happen to the price? Who would gain and who would lose?

check.q: Why were spices so expensive in Europe?
choices: They were carried a long way and sold many times
check.why: Spices came from Asia over long routes, and each merchant along the way raised the price.

check.q: What was Columbus's idea?
choices: To sail west across the ocean to reach Asia
check.why: Columbus believed Asia was not far to the west and that he could reach it by sailing across the Atlantic.

check.q: Which was NOT one of the main reasons Europeans sailed west?
choices: To find a cheaper route for trade
check.why: The reasons were trade, gold, land and religion. Learning Native languages was not a goal.

lessons.title: What 1492 Set in Motion
lessons.mainIdea: Columbus landed in the Caribbean in 1492 believing he had reached Asia, and his voyage started centuries of contact that changed both worlds.
reading: On October 12, 1492, after about five weeks at sea, three Spanish ships reached a small island in the Bahamas. Columbus went ashore and claimed it for the king and queen of Spain. The people who lived there, the *Taíno*, came out to meet the strangers. Columbus thought he had reached islands near India, so he called the people Indians. The name stuck, though it was a mistake.

Columbus wrote in his journal that the Taíno were gentle and generous. They brought parrots, cotton thread and food. In the same pages, he wrote that they would make good servants and could be easily ruled. He took some Taíno back to Spain by force. On later trips, the Spanish made Taíno people dig for gold. Within a few decades, war, hunger and disease had killed most of the Taíno on the islands.

Columbus never reached Asia and never understood that he had found continents unknown to Europe. But his voyage changed history. Ships began to cross the Atlantic every year. Plants, animals, people, ideas and diseases moved in both directions. Historians call this the *Columbian Exchange*. The next lessons show what it carried.

words.d: the people who lived on the islands of the Caribbean when Columbus arrived
the movement of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492

look.title: Columbus Writes About the Taíno
look.text: In his journal for October 1492, Columbus described the people he met as friendly and eager to trade. He wrote that they gave whatever they had and asked for little. He also wrote that they had no iron weapons, and that with a small number of armed men he could take control of them all and make them do whatever he wished.
look.cite: Journal of Christopher Columbus, October 1492 (paraphrased from later copies)
look.prompt: Columbus praised the Taíno and, in the same breath, planned to rule them. What does this tell you about how he saw them?

check.q: Why did Columbus call the people he met Indians?
choices: He thought he was near India
It was the name of the island
check.why: Columbus believed he had reached islands near India in Asia, so he used that name.

check.q: What happened to most of the Taíno within a few decades?
choices: They died from war, hunger and disease
check.why: Forced labor, war and new diseases killed most of the Taíno on the islands.

check.q: What is the Columbian Exchange?
choices: The movement of plants, animals, people and diseases across the Atlantic after 1492
A trade between Columbus and the king
check.why: After 1492, living things moved in both directions between the Americas and the rest of the world.

lessons.title: Corn Goes East, Wheat Goes West
lessons.mainIdea: Foods from the Americas fed the world, and animals and crops from Europe changed the Americas.
reading: Look at a pizza. The wheat crust and the cheese came from Europe. The tomato sauce came from the Americas. Before 1492, no one in Italy had ever seen a *tomato*. No one in Ireland had seen a potato. No one in Africa had grown corn. No one in Mexico had eaten a cow or tasted wheat bread. The Columbian Exchange put them all on one plate.

Native farmers had bred corn, potatoes, tomatoes, peppers, beans, squash, peanuts, cacao for chocolate and many more plants over thousands of years. Once these crossed the ocean, they fed millions. Potatoes grow well in cold, poor soil, so they became the main food of Ireland and northern Europe. Corn spread across Africa and China. The population of the world grew partly because of American crops.

Going the other way came wheat, rice, sugar cane, coffee, bananas and fruit trees. Also animals: cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, chickens and horses. The Americas had no large farm animals before this except the llama. Pigs and cattle ran wild and multiplied. They also trampled Native cornfields. Sugar cane grew so well in the Caribbean that Europeans built huge farms, and soon they were bringing enslaved Africans by force to work them.

words.d: a plant first grown in the Americas that became a key food in Europe after 1492
a tall grass grown for sugar, brought to the Americas and grown on large farms with enslaved labor

look.title: Two Dinner Tables in 1491
look.text: In a village in Italy, a family eats bread, cheese, cabbage and a little pork. There is no tomato, no potato, no corn, no chocolate. In a village in Mexico, a family eats corn tortillas, beans, squash, peppers and turkey. There is no beef, no wheat, no cheese, no sugar, no rice.
look.prompt: Pick one food you ate this week. Was it from the Americas, from the rest of the world, or a mix? Could you have eaten it in 1491 where you live?

check.q: Which food came from the Americas to Europe?
check.why: Potatoes were bred by farmers in South America and became a main food in Europe.

check.q: Why did potatoes become so important in Ireland?
choices: They grow well in cold, poor soil
The Spanish forced people to eat them
check.why: Potatoes give a lot of food from small, cold fields, which fit northern Europe.

check.q: What was one harmful effect of sugar cane in the Caribbean?
choices: Europeans brought enslaved Africans by force to grow it
It made the islands too sweet
check.why: Sugar farms needed huge amounts of labor, and Europeans met it with enslaved people taken from Africa.

lessons.title: The Horse Changes the Plains
lessons.mainIdea: Horses brought by the Spanish spread north and turned Plains peoples into fast-moving hunters and riders within about two hundred years.
reading: There were no horses in the Americas when Columbus landed. The Spanish brought them to Mexico in 1519. Native people had never seen anything like them. Some Spanish soldiers on horseback seemed at first to be one giant animal. But soon Native peoples learned to ride, and they learned fast. Horses escaped or were traded, and they spread north across the land.

For Plains peoples, the horse was a revolution. Before, a family could carry only what their dogs could pull. Hunting bison on foot was slow and dangerous. On horseback, a hunter could ride into a herd and pick the animal he wanted. Tipis grew bigger, because horses could haul longer poles. Families could move farther and faster. Nations like the Comanche and Lakota became some of the best riders in the world.

The horse also brought conflict. Nations moved onto the Plains that had never lived there before. They competed for hunting grounds and for horses. Raids to take horses became common. By the 1700s, before most Plains people had ever met a white settler, their lives had already been changed by a European animal. That is how the Columbian Exchange worked: its effects ran ahead of the Europeans themselves.

words.d: a change so big that it turns a way of life upside down
a Plains nation famous for its skill with horses in the 1700s and 1800s

look.title: The Horse Moves North
rows: Pueblo Revolt frees thousands of horses
Comanche riding on the southern Plains, about
Lakota riding on the northern Plains, about
look.cite: Standard dates used by historians of the Plains, rounded
look.prompt: About how long did it take horses to travel from Mexico to the northern Plains? How did they get there without Spanish riders?

check.q: Where did the horses of the Plains come from?
choices: They came north from the Spanish in Mexico
The English brought them to the Plains
check.why: The Spanish brought horses to Mexico in 1519, and they spread north by escape and trade.

check.q: How did horses change bison hunting?
choices: Riders could pick out an animal and chase it
Horses scared the bison away for good
check.why: Riding into a herd was far faster and safer than hunting on foot.

check.q: What does it mean that the Exchange 'ran ahead of the Europeans'?
choices: Plains life changed because of horses before most Plains people met Europeans
check.why: Horses spread across the Plains by the 1700s, long before white settlers arrived there.

lessons.title: Sickness Crosses the Sea
lessons.mainIdea: Diseases from Europe killed more Native people than any war, because no one in the Americas had ever been exposed to them.
reading: The deadliest thing on the European ships was invisible. It was *germs*. Smallpox, measles and the flu had lived in Europe, Asia and Africa for thousands of years. People there often caught them as children. Many died, but many survived and could not catch the disease again. That is called *immunity*. No one in the Americas had ever met these germs. No one had immunity.

When smallpox reached a Native village, nearly everyone got sick at the same time. There was no one healthy to bring water or food. In 1520, smallpox reached the great Aztec city of Tenochtitlan in Mexico. It killed the emperor and a large share of the people. The Spanish captured the weakened city the next year. Disease did more to defeat the Aztecs than Spanish steel.

Sickness spread along trade routes faster than Europeans traveled. Some villages lost most of their people before they ever saw a European. Historians do not agree on exact numbers, but they agree that a very large share of Native people died in the first two centuries after 1492. It was one of the greatest losses of life in human history. The survivors rebuilt, but their world was smaller and their nations weaker when the settlers came.

words.d: tiny living things that cause disease and spread from person to person
the body's ability to fight off a disease it has met before

look.title: A Village After the Sickness
look.text: A French priest walks into a village on a river in the 1600s. Last year it held five hundred people. Now the corn stands unharvested. Many houses are empty. The people left are mostly old and very young. An elder tells him that the sickness came from traders upriver, before any Frenchman had set foot here.
look.prompt: How could a disease reach a village before any European did? What would this do to a nation's ability to defend its land?

check.q: Why did European diseases kill so many Native people?
choices: Native people had never met these germs and had no immunity
The diseases were new in Europe too
check.why: Immunity comes from having met a germ before. No one in the Americas had, so nearly everyone got sick at once.

check.q: What helped the Spanish capture Tenochtitlan in 1521?
choices: Smallpox had killed a large share of the city's people
check.why: Smallpox reached the city in 1520 and killed the emperor and many others, weakening it before the Spanish attack.

check.q: Why could a village lose people to disease before meeting any European?
choices: The disease came through the air from Europe
Germs spread along Native trade routes
The disease came from the bison
check.why: Traders carried germs from village to village along routes that were already old.

lessons.title: Spanish Soldiers and Missions
lessons.mainIdea: The Spanish conquered Native empires, forced people to work and built missions to change their religion, and in 1680 the Pueblo people drove them out.
reading: The Spanish came first and came to rule. In 1519 a soldier named Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with a few hundred men. With horses, steel, guns, smallpox and thousands of Native allies who hated the Aztecs, he captured Tenochtitlan in 1521. Spain took the Aztec gold and silver and ruled Mexico for three hundred years. Spanish soldiers who conquered are called *conquistadors*.

In the lands they took, the Spanish gave Native villages to Spanish settlers. The villagers had to work for the settler and pay him. Priests built *missions*, churches with farms around them, and required Native people to live there, work and become Christians. Some priests protected the people from the worst abuse. Many did not. Native religions were banned, and ceremonies were punished.

The Pueblo peoples of New Mexico put up with this for about eighty years. Then in 1680, a religious leader named Popé sent runners to every pueblo with knotted cords. The knots counted the days until the uprising. On the chosen day the pueblos rose together, killed hundreds of Spanish and drove the rest out of New Mexico. The Spanish did not return for twelve years. The Pueblo Revolt is the most successful Native uprising against Europeans in what is now the United States.

words.d: a Spanish soldier who conquered lands in the Americas in the 1500s
a church and farm where priests required Native people to live, work and become Christians
the 1680 uprising in which the Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out of New Mexico

look.title: The Knotted Cord
look.text: A runner arrives at a pueblo out of breath. He hands the leader a cord of yucca fiber with several knots. Each morning the leader unties one knot. When the last knot is gone, every pueblo across New Mexico will rise on the same day. The runner speaks a different language from this pueblo, but the knots need no words.
look.prompt: Why did Popé use knotted cords instead of a written message? What problems did he solve by having every pueblo act on the same day?

check.q: What helped Cortés capture Tenochtitlan besides horses and guns?
choices: Smallpox and thousands of Native allies
The Aztecs surrendered without a fight
check.why: Disease weakened the city, and Native nations who hated Aztec rule joined the Spanish.

check.q: What was a mission?
choices: A church and farm where Native people were made to live, work and become Christians
check.why: Missions combined a church with farms and required Native people to change their religion and work there.

check.q: What happened in the Pueblo Revolt of 1680?
choices: The Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out for twelve years
check.why: Led by Popé, the pueblos rose together and pushed the Spanish out of New Mexico until 1692.

lessons.title: French Traders on the Rivers
lessons.mainIdea: The French came in small numbers to trade furs, so they relied on Native alliances, learned Native languages and often married into Native families, including in Illinois.
reading: The French did things differently. Few French people wanted to move across the ocean. Those who came wanted beaver fur, which sold for high prices in Europe for hats. To get fur, they needed Native hunters. So the French built trading posts, not big farms. They learned Native languages. Many French traders married Native women, and their children grew up in both worlds.

In 1673 a priest named Jacques Marquette and a trader named Louis Jolliet paddled down the Mississippi River. They were the first French to see Illinois. The Illinois people welcomed them with the *calumet*, a long peace pipe. On the way home they went up the Illinois River, past a village of thousands near where Utica is today. Marquette wrote that the land was rich and the people kind.

Soon French forts and missions dotted the rivers. La Salle built a fort near Peoria in 1680. The town of Kaskaskia in southern Illinois started as a French mission in 1703. Illinois hunters brought furs, and French traders brought kettles, cloth, guns and brandy. The French also brought disease and drew the Illinois into wars against the Iroquois and others. But French and Native people in Illinois lived side by side for nearly a century, and many families were both.

words.d: the exchange of animal furs, especially beaver, for European goods like kettles and cloth
a long decorated pipe smoked to show peace and friendship

look.title: Marquette Meets the Illinois
look.text: In his journal, Marquette wrote that when he and Jolliet came to a village of the Illinois in 1673, an elder came out to greet them with his hands raised toward the sun. The elder said that the sun was beautiful because the French had come to visit, and he invited them into the village in peace. They were given a feast and a calumet to carry as a sign of safe passage.
look.cite: Jacques Marquette, journal of the 1673 voyage (paraphrased from a later printed version)
look.prompt: This is the French side of the meeting. What might an Illinois elder have written about the same day, if he had kept a journal?

check.q: Why did the French need Native allies more than the Spanish did?
choices: Few French came, and they depended on Native hunters for furs
The French did not want land
check.why: The fur trade only worked with Native hunters, so the French built alliances instead of conquering.

check.q: Who were the first French to see Illinois?
check.why: Marquette and Jolliet paddled down the Mississippi and up the Illinois River in 1673.

check.q: What was the calumet?
choices: A peace pipe offered to guests
check.why: The long pipe was smoked to show peace, and carrying one gave safe passage among nations.

lessons.title: English Farms and Fences
lessons.mainIdea: The English came as families to farm, so they took more land than the Spanish or French, and land became the main cause of war.
reading: The English came last and came to stay. Jamestown in Virginia began in 1607. Plymouth in Massachusetts began in 1620. Unlike the French, English settlers came by the thousands, as whole families. They wanted farms of their own. They cleared forests, built fences and let cattle and pigs roam. Every new farm was land that a Native nation had used for hunting, fishing or planting.

At first, Native nations helped. The Powhatan people traded corn to starving Jamestown. The Wampanoag leader Massasoit made a treaty with Plymouth and shared a harvest feast with them in 1621. But the English kept coming. The two sides also thought about land differently. To Native peoples, land was shared by a nation for use. To the English, land was *property* that one person owned and could fence and sell.

Within fifty years the friendship broke. In 1675 Massasoit's son Metacom, called King Philip by the English, led many nations against the settlers. The war burned dozens of towns on both sides. Thousands died. The English won, and Metacom was killed. After that, the pattern in English lands was set: settlers moved in, the *frontier* moved west, and Native nations were pushed off the land.

words.d: something owned by one person, who can fence it, keep others out or sell it
the edge of the land settled by Europeans, which kept moving west

look.title: Who Settled Where, and When
rows: Spanish found Santa Fe, New Mexico
look.prompt: Put the three countries in order of who arrived first in what is now the United States. Which reached Illinois?

check.q: How were English settlers different from French traders?
choices: The English came as farming families and took much more land
The English came in small numbers
The English married into Native families more often
check.why: Thousands of English families came to farm, and each farm meant land taken from a Native nation.

check.q: How did the English and Native peoples see land differently?
choices: Native nations shared land for use; the English saw it as property to own and sell
The English shared land; Native nations sold it
check.why: This difference led to endless misunderstanding and conflict about what a land deal meant.

check.q: Who was Metacom?
choices: Massasoit's son, who led a war against the English in 1675
check.why: The English called him King Philip. His war was the last big attempt to push the English out of New England.

sections.title: Loss, Resistance and Points of View

lessons.title: Land Lost, Lives Lost
lessons.mainIdea: Over three centuries, Native nations lost most of their land and many of their people through disease, war and treaties, including here in Illinois.
reading: Add it up. Disease killed a very large share of Native people. Wars killed more. Then came *treaties*, written agreements between a Native nation and a government. On paper, a treaty was a deal between equals. In practice, nations weakened by sickness and war often signed because they had no better choice. Many treaties were broken as soon as settlers wanted more land.

Illinois shows the whole story. When Marquette came in 1673, the Illinois people numbered many thousands in big villages. Disease and wars with other nations shrank them. In 1803 the Kaskaskia, one of the Illinois nations, signed a treaty giving up most of their land to the United States. The Sauk leader Black Hawk tried to return to his village on the Rock River in 1832. Soldiers and militia drove his people out in a short, brutal war.

In 1833, at a treaty signed in Chicago, the Potawatomi gave up their remaining land in northern Illinois. Within a few years they were marched west. By the 1840s almost no Native nation held land in Illinois. The state was named for a people who were no longer allowed to live in it. That was the cost of the encounter, paid by the people who were here first.

words.d: a written agreement between a Native nation and a government, often about land
ordinary citizens who serve as part-time soldiers

look.title: Black Hawk Remembers the Rock River
look.text: In the story of his life, told in 1833 after his defeat, Black Hawk said that the land along the Rock River was a beautiful country. He said he loved his town, his cornfields and the home of his people, and that he had fought for it. He asked what people would think of a man who did not fight for the place where his family was buried.
look.cite: Black Hawk, Life of Black Hawk, told to an interpreter, 1833 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Black Hawk was defeated, yet he was asked to tell his story and it was printed. Why might it matter that his side was written down at all?

check.q: What is a treaty?
choices: A written agreement between a nation and a government
check.why: Treaties were the legal way land passed from Native nations to the United States, though many were unfair or broken.

check.q: Why did weakened nations often sign treaties giving up land?
choices: They had little choice after disease and war
The treaties gave them more land
check.why: Nations shrunk by sickness and fighting could not hold off settlers and often signed to survive.

check.q: What happened to the Potawatomi after the 1833 treaty in Chicago?
choices: They were marched west within a few years
They moved to Canada and returned
check.why: The treaty gave up their remaining land in northern Illinois, and they were removed west.

lessons.title: Resisting and Adapting
lessons.mainIdea: Native peoples fought back, made alliances, took up new tools and kept their languages and ceremonies alive, and they are still doing so.
reading: Native nations were never just victims. They chose, planned and fought. The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 drove out an empire. Metacom nearly did the same in New England. In 1763 an Ottawa leader named Pontiac united nations around the Great Lakes and captured most of the British forts west of the mountains. Illinois nations joined him. The British had to promise that settlers would stay east of the mountains, though the promise was soon broken.

Nations also adapted, which means changing to fit new conditions. They took the horse and became the finest riders on Earth. They took iron, guns and cloth and made them their own. Some nations played the French, Spanish and English against each other to protect their land. Native leaders learned to read treaties and argue in court. Adapting was not giving up. It was survival.

The hardest thing to protect was *culture*: language, ceremony, story. Governments and missions worked for centuries to stamp these out. Yet the Haudenosaunee still hold council. The Hopi still plant corn the old way. Native languages are being taught again to children in Illinois and across the country. The Illinois language itself, called Miami-Illinois, is being relearned from old French dictionaries. Resistance did not end. It changed shape.

words.d: to change how you live so you can survive new conditions
a people's language, beliefs, ceremonies, stories and ways of living

look.title: A Word Comes Back
look.text: In a classroom in the 2000s, a girl practices a word from the Miami-Illinois language. Her great-great-grandparents spoke it every day. Then it stopped being spoken. Now a scholar has rebuilt the language from dictionaries that French priests wrote three hundred years ago. The girl says the word for river out loud. It has not been spoken in that room for a very long time.
look.prompt: Why might a language matter so much to a nation? How is learning it again a kind of resistance?

check.q: What did Pontiac do in 1763?
choices: United Great Lakes nations and captured most British forts in the west
check.why: Pontiac's alliance took most British forts west of the mountains and forced a promise to hold back settlers.

check.q: Which is an example of adapting?
choices: Refusing to ever use metal tools
Learning to ride horses and read treaties
check.why: Adapting means taking new tools and skills to survive, not giving up who you are.

check.q: How is the Miami-Illinois language being relearned?
choices: From dictionaries written by French priests long ago
check.why: French priests in the 1700s wrote down the language, and scholars are using those pages to bring it back.

lessons.title: Same Event, Different Stories
lessons.mainIdea: The same event looks different depending on who tells it, so good historians read more than one side and ask who wrote a source and why.
reading: Here is one event. In 1621 Wampanoag men and English settlers at Plymouth ate together after the harvest. For many Americans, this is the first Thanksgiving, a happy story of sharing. For many Wampanoag today, the same day is the start of a story that ends with their land taken and their nation nearly destroyed. Both are talking about the same meal. Both are telling the truth about part of it.

That is why a *point of view* matters. A point of view is the position a person sees from. A Spanish soldier, a Spanish priest, an Aztec warrior and an Aztec farmer would each describe the fall of Tenochtitlan differently. Most written records from this time were made by Europeans. Native accounts were spoken, painted or remembered. To hear them, historians have to look harder.

Good readers ask three questions about any *source*. Who made it? When? Why? Columbus wrote his journal to impress the king and queen who paid for his trip. Black Hawk told his story to explain himself after losing a war. Neither one is lying, but each has a reason to tell it his way. Today some places mark the second Monday of October as Columbus Day, and others call it Indigenous Peoples' Day. That argument is about which story we choose to remember.

words.d: the position a person sees an event from, which shapes how they describe it
a record from the past, such as a journal, letter, painting or spoken story

look.title: Two Reports of One Trade
look.text: A French trader writes home: 'Today I traded one kettle and two knives for twelve fine beaver pelts. A very good bargain.' The same evening an Illinois hunter tells his family: 'Today I traded twelve pelts, which took me all winter, for a kettle that will last my wife ten years and knives that will feed us. A very good bargain.'
look.prompt: Both think they won. Is one of them wrong? What could a historian learn by reading both accounts instead of one?

check.q: Why do the Wampanoag and many other Americans tell the 1621 harvest feast differently?
choices: One side is making it up
They are describing the same event from different points of view
check.why: Both describe a real meal, but what happened afterward shapes how each side remembers it.

check.q: Why are there fewer written Native accounts from this time?
choices: Native people had nothing to say
Native accounts were mostly spoken, painted or remembered, not written
Native people wrote only in Spanish
check.why: Most Native nations kept history by oral tradition and art, so historians must look beyond written pages.

check.q: What three questions should you ask about a source?
choices: Is it long, is it old, is it famous?
Is it true, is it false, is it fun?
Who made it, when, and why?
Where is it kept, who owns it, how much is it worth?
check.why: Knowing the maker, the time and the purpose tells you what point of view shaped the source.

review.q: What was the main reason Europeans first wanted a sea route to Asia?
choices: To buy spices and silk more cheaply
review.why: Asian goods were very costly after passing through many merchants, and a direct route would cut the price.

review.q: Which of these traveled from the Americas to the rest of the world?
review.why: American crops fed the world. Horses, cattle, wheat, sugar and the diseases came the other way.

review.q: Which killed the most Native people after 1492?
review.why: Native people had no immunity, and epidemics killed a very large share of the population.

review.q: Which country relied most on fur trade and Native alliances?
review.why: Few French came, and they depended on Native hunters for the beaver furs they wanted.

review.q: Why did the English take more Native land than the French?
choices: English families came by the thousands to farm
review.why: Each new farm took land that a Native nation had used, and English settlers kept coming.

review.q: What did the Pueblo Revolt and Pontiac's war have in common?
choices: Both were led by the Spanish
Both were Native nations uniting to push Europeans out
Both ended with treaties in Chicago
review.why: In 1680 and 1763, many communities acted together to drive out or hold back a European power.

review.q: What happened to Native nations in Illinois by the 1840s?
choices: They had signed treaties and been removed west
They had joined the state government
They had grown to their largest size
review.why: Treaties in 1803 and 1833, and the Black Hawk War of 1832, ended with almost no Native land left in Illinois.

review.q: Why should a historian read both Columbus's journal and a Native account of 1492?
choices: Because Native accounts are always correct
Because each shows a different point of view on the same event
review.why: Every source has a maker, a time and a purpose, and comparing sources gives a fuller picture.
